sections.model_projection: The model projects San Diego State 24.7, UCLA 23.99, a near-pick-em with UCLA holding a razor-thin 0.71-point home edge. UCLA's win probability sits at 48.35%, essentially a coin flip. The projected total of 48.69 sits 4.8 points under the market number of 53.5. The market has UCLA as an 11.5-point favorite, a significant 12.2-point gap from the model's margin.
sections.offensive_matchup: UCLA's offense carries a clear rushing advantage, ranking 2nd in opponent-adjusted rushing EPA per play (0.35) and 7th in offensive line yards (3.51), while SDSU's run defense grades out as only average at 15th in defensive rushing EPA allowed. However, UCLA's passing attack is a genuine liability — their opponent-adjusted passing EPA per play of 0.19 ranks 113th, and they run a neutral-script pass rate of 54%, meaning they'll be asked to throw in neutral situations against an SDSU pass defense that ranks 13th in defensive passing EPA allowed (0.054). SDSU's offense is run-heavy (pass rate of just 38%, ranking 128th) and struggles to move the chains consistently, ranking 98th in offensive success rate (40.5%), which measures the share of plays that gain enough yards to stay on schedule. The Aztecs' offensive efficiency is largely dependent on their ground game, where they rank 64th in rushing EPA per play, a middling number that will be tested by a UCLA defensive front that, while not elite, is serviceable.
sections.quarterback_edge: UCLA's Nico Iamaleava holds a modest edge over SDSU's Jayden Denegal based on career volume and efficiency. Iamaleava has 674 career attempts across 25 games with a 64.8% completion rate and 7.1 yards per attempt, while Denegal has 266 attempts across 13 games at 59.8% completion and 7.51 yards per attempt — Denegal's per-attempt number is slightly higher, but the experience gap is meaningful. Neither quarterback has a career EPA per dropback on file, limiting the depth of this comparison. The model gives UCLA a slight edge here worth 0.16 points toward the Bruins.
sections.trenches: The offensive line matchup strongly favors UCLA — their line yards figure of 3.51 (7th nationally) faces an SDSU defensive front that ranks 121st in havoc rate (disruption plays per snap), meaning the Bruins should be able to establish a physical run game. Conversely, SDSU's offensive line (line yards rank 28th, sack rate allowed rank 76th) faces a UCLA defensive front that ranks 130th in sack rate, so the Aztecs' protection should be adequate even if UCLA won't generate consistent pressure. The defensive front edge favors SDSU in the model's scoring, largely because SDSU's pass defense is elite (13th in defensive passing EPA allowed) and their run defense is solid, while UCLA's defense has struggled to stop the run (110th in defensive rushing EPA allowed at 0.159). The net trench battle is a split: UCLA wins the run-blocking matchup, SDSU wins the defensive front matchup.
sections.explosive_play_edge: SDSU's defense is one of the nation's best at preventing big plays, ranking 7th in explosive plays allowed (7.45% of opponent snaps), which directly threatens UCLA's most dangerous offensive weapon — their explosive play rate of 13.9% (35th) and raw explosiveness figure of 1.19. UCLA's offense generated a 22.6% explosive play rate in raw numbers last week, but that came against a weaker opponent (SOS rank 184 vs. SDSU's 115), and the opponent-adjusted figure drops to 13.9%. SDSU's ability to limit chunk plays is the single biggest defensive asset they bring into this game, and it could neutralize UCLA's most efficient offensive avenue.
sections.third_down_red_zone: SDSU holds a commanding third-down edge: their defense allows opponents to convert just 33.1% of third downs (28th nationally), while UCLA's defense surrenders conversions at a 54.5% rate (134th — nearly worst in the country). SDSU's own third-down offense is mediocre at 35.4% (106th), but the defensive advantage is so lopsided it dominates the category. In the red zone, SDSU's defense allows touchdowns on only 46.6% of opponent trips (9th), compared to UCLA's defense giving up touchdowns on 82.95% of trips (130th) — note these are flagged as low-sample figures after one game. SDSU's red zone offense converts at a 76.6% TD rate (30th), creating a scenario where if the Aztecs reach the red zone, they are likely to score touchdowns against a UCLA defense that has struggled to hold in that area.
sections.roster_talent: UCLA holds a talent edge by roster rating percentile (57th vs. SDSU's 45th) and carries a 14% blue-chip ratio over four years while SDSU has a 0% blue-chip ratio, meaning UCLA has more highly recruited players on the roster. However, SDSU has a significantly higher continuity index (0.71 vs. UCLA's 0.52), reflecting more returning production across the roster — SDSU returns 69% of total production versus UCLA's 60%. UCLA also underwent a head coaching change, adding uncertainty to how their talent translates under a new system, while SDSU's coaching staff is unchanged.
sections.recent_form: Both teams have played exactly one game, so recent form data is limited to a single-game sample with no multi-game trend available. SDSU scored 53 points in Week 1 (raw) but allowed 20, while UCLA scored 45 and allowed 24. The model registers no form shift for either team. Given the single-game sample and the disparity in strength of schedule (SDSU faced a rank-115 opponent, UCLA faced a rank-184 opponent), these raw results carry limited predictive weight.
sections.market_movement: The spread opened at UCLA -8.5 and has moved to -11.5, a 3-point shift toward the home team on DraftKings. That movement crosses the key number of 10, which is a structurally significant threshold in college football. The total has held steady at 53.5 with no movement. The model's projected margin of -0.71 (essentially a pick) sits 12.2 points away from the current market spread of -11.5, one of the larger model-vs-market divergences possible. Public betting percentages are unavailable, so the cause of the line movement cannot be attributed to any specific source.

sections.expected_game_script: UCLA will likely try to establish their elite run game early — their offensive line and rushing EPA numbers suggest they can move the ball on the ground against SDSU's average run defense, and doing so would keep SDSU's offense off the field and limit their low-volume, run-heavy attack. SDSU, in turn, will lean on their ground game and ball-control approach (62 plays per game, 28-second pace) to keep possessions long and avoid falling into a passing situation where their 128th-ranked pass rate becomes a liability. The critical tension is whether SDSU's elite pass defense can neutralize UCLA's passing game enough to keep the Aztecs' offense in manageable down-and-distance situations, given that SDSU's own third-down offense converts at only 35.4%. Red zone possessions figure to be decisive: if SDSU reaches the red zone, their 76.6% TD rate against UCLA's porous red zone defense (82.95% TD rate allowed) could produce outsized scoring. UCLA's home field advantage and talent edge provide a structural cushion, but the model sees this as far closer than the 11.5-point market spread implies, projecting a near-even game with SDSU covering significant ground through defensive efficiency and situational football.
